content: All household members and close contacts of individuals with tuberculosis (TB) who exhibit symptoms consistent with TB disease may be offered counseling and testing for HIV as part of their clinical evaluation. This is a conditional recommendation based on very low certainty of evidence. Additionally, all household contacts of an index case who is living with HIV should be counseled and tested for HIV. This is a strong recommendation, also based on very low certainty of evidence. The prevention of TB in children and adolescents is guided by consolidated recommendations from the World Health Organization (WHO). These recommendations are derived from guidelines on TB infection prevention and control, a position paper on Bacillus Calmette-Guérin (BCG) vaccination, and guidelines on tuberculosis preventive treatment (TPT). For detailed information on the evidence, justification, subgroups, implementation, and monitoring considerations, the source guidelines or WHO’s TB Knowledge Sharing Platform should be consulted. WHO recommends administrative controls to reduce the transmission of Mycobacterium tuberculosis in healthcare settings. Respiratory isolation of individuals with presumed or confirmed infectious TB is also recommended to reduce transmission. Prompt initiation of effective TB treatment is strongly recommended to reduce transmission risks. Additionally, respiratory hygiene practices, such as cough etiquette, are advised for individuals with presumed or confirmed TB. Environmental controls, such as upper-room germicidal ultraviolet (GUV) systems and ventilation systems (natural, mixed-mode, mechanical, or with high-efficiency particulate air [HEPA] filters), are conditionally recommended to reduce TB transmission in high-risk settings. The use of particulate respirators within a respiratory protection program is also conditionally recommended for healthcare workers and others in high-risk environments. BCG vaccination is recommended for neonates in countries with high TB or leprosy incidence. A single dose should be administered at birth or as soon as possible thereafter. If missed at birth, catch-up vaccination is recommended at the earliest opportunity. Co-administration of BCG with the hepatitis B birth dose is safe and strongly recommended. In low-incidence countries, selective BCG vaccination may be considered for neonates in high-risk groups, such as those with close contacts who have a history of TB or leprosy or those with household connections to high-incidence regions. Revaccination with BCG is not recommended, as studies show minimal or no additional benefit. For HIV-infected infants, BCG vaccination should be delayed until antiretroviral therapy (ART) has been initiated and the infant is clinically and immunologically stable. TB preventive treatment (TPT) is recommended for individuals at risk of TB infection, including people living with HIV, household contacts of TB patients, and other high-risk groups. Adults and adolescents living with HIV who are unlikely to have active TB disease should receive TPT as part of comprehensive HIV care, regardless of ART status, pregnancy, or previous TB treatment. Infants and children living with HIV who are in contact with a TB patient and are unlikely to have TB disease should also receive TPT. Household contacts of bacteriologically confirmed pulmonary TB cases, particularly children under 5 years of age, should be given TPT even if TB infection testing is unavailable. In high-risk settings, TPT may also be considered for selected household contacts of multidrug-resistant TB patients based on individualized risk assessment. Systematic TB infection testing and treatment are recommended for individuals initiating anti-TNF treatment, those receiving dialysis, those preparing for organ or hematological transplants, and those with silicosis. Testing and treatment may also be considered for prisoners, healthcare workers, immigrants from high TB burden countries, homeless individuals, and people who use drugs. However, systematic testing and treatment are not recommended for individuals with diabetes, harmful alcohol use, tobacco use, or underweight status unless they belong to other high-risk groups. For diagnosing TB in children and adolescents, WHO recommends the use of the Xpert MTB/RIF Ultra assay as the initial diagnostic test for pulmonary TB and rifampicin resistance. This test can be performed on sputum, nasopharyngeal aspirate, gastric aspirate, or stool specimens. The assay is preferred over smear microscopy, culture, and phenotypic drug susceptibility testing due to its higher sensitivity and specificity. However, a negative test result does not exclude TB disease, and clinical judgment should guide further evaluation and treatment decisions.
